lessons.title: Reading the Quran: Arabic Alphabets (Huroof) and Diacritical Marks (Harakaat)
lessons.notes_html:
Reading the Holy Quran

The first part of this chapter teaches us to read the Holy Quran correctly. For correct reading, we must first know the Arabic Alphabets and their marks.

Arabic Alphabets (Huroof-e-Hijaa)

  • There are 29 Arabic Alphabets, called Huroof-e-Hijaa.
  • Another name of these alphabets is Huroof-e-TaHajji.
  • These alphabets (huroof) are joined together to make words.
  • The 29 huroof in order are: ا ب ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ع غ ف ق ک ل م ن و ہ ء ی

Letters Without Dots

Some huroof have dots (nuqta) and some have no dots at all. Five huroof which have no dots are: Alif (ا), Haa (ح), Daal (د), Seen (س) and Kaaf (ک).

  • Tha is spelled as ثا, just as Baa is spelled with Alif.
  • Suad is written as ص, Seen is written as س and Tha is written as ث.
  • The harf which comes just before Meem (م) is Laam (ل).

Key Points

  • Arabic Alphabets are 29 in number and are also called Huroof-e-TaHajji.
  • Huroof join together to make words.
  • Alif, Haa, Daal, Seen and Kaaf have no dots (nuqta).

mcqs.why: Suad is written as ص. The book explains that س is Seen and ث is Tha, so they cannot be Suad.

mcqs.why: In the order of the huroof-e-hijaa, Laam (ل) comes just before Meem (م), so the correct answer is Laam.

mcqs.q: Tha is spelled as:
mcqs.why: The book states that Tha is spelled as ثا, just as Baa is spelled with Alif.

mcqs.why: The book says that the 29 alphabets (huroof) are joined together to make words, which is how the words of the Holy Quran are formed.

mcqs.why: Seen (س) is one of the five huroof without dots listed in the book: Alif, Haa, Daal, Seen and Kaaf. Sheen, Jeem and Taa all carry dots.

mcqs.why: In the chart of the Arabic Alphabets, Haa (ح) comes just after Jeem (ج) and before Khaa (خ).

mcqs.why: The chart of the huroof-e-hijaa ends with Yaa (ی), which is the 29th and last harf of the Arabic Alphabets.

lessons.title: Diacritical Marks (Harakaat / I'raab) and Jazm
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Harkat?

Harkat means movement or motion. The signs zabar, zair and pesh are called harakat or I'raab. If any harkat is placed on a letter (harf), that harf is said to be Mutaharrik, because there is a movement in the voice of the speaker while pronouncing it.

Other Names of the Harakaat

  • Zabar is also called Fat-ha.
  • Zair is also called Kasra.
  • Pesh is also called Dhamma / Zamma.

Jazm (Sukoon)

The symbol ( ْ ) is called Jazm. A letter which has a Jazm upon it is known as Majzoom. Jazm is also known as sukoon, and the majzoom harf is also called 'saakin'. Jazm or sukoon can never be placed on the first harf of a word.

Reading the Harakaat in Words

  • In اَلْفَتْحُ, the huroof with Zabar are Hamza (Alif) and Faa, and the harf with Pesh is Haa.
  • In كَبُرَ, the huroof with Zabar are Kaaf and Raa, and the harf with Pesh is Baa.
  • In عَبَدَ, the huroof 'Aien, Baa and Daal all carry Zabar.
  • In عُقِدَ, Daal has Zabar, Qaaf has Zair and 'Aien has Pesh.

Joining and Breaking Huroof

Separate huroof can be joined together to write a word, like كِتَابٌ. In the same way, a joined word can be broken into its separate huroof; for example, اَلْحَمْدُ is made of the separate huroof Alif, Laam, Haa, Meem and Daal.

Key Points

  • Zabar, zair and pesh are the harakat (I'raab); a harf carrying one of them is Mutaharrik.
  • Zabar = Fat-ha, Zair = Kasra, Pesh = Dhamma / Zamma.
  • A harf with Jazm (sukoon) on it is called Majzoom.

lessons.title: Tanveen, Khara Zabar, Khari Zair and Ulta Pesh
lessons.notes_html:
What is Tanveen?

Tanveen means the double harakat: double zabar ( ً ), double zair ( ٍ ) and double pesh ( ٌ ). When a tanveen is used, the sound of Noon Sakin is produced. For example, double zabar over Taa is read as 'Tann'. Tanveen is always placed on the last letter (harf) of a word, as in كِتَابٌ and نَفْسٍ.

Khara Zabar (Standing Zabar)

Khara Zabar is a type of zabar, but its pronunciation is stretched more than the zabar. Because of this, it sounds like an alif when pronounced, and in place of a Khara Zabar a small symbol of alif is placed.

Khari Zair and Ulta Pesh

  • Khari Zair is the standing (vertical) zair, written in the place of zair, as in بِهٖ.
  • Ulta Pesh (upside-down pesh) is a type of pesh. Its pronunciation is stretched, so it sounds like a stretched Wow (waaw) when pronounced.

Key Points

  • Tanveen = double zabar, double zair and double pesh; it produces the sound of Noon Sakin.
  • Khara Zabar is stretched and sounds like an alif.
  • Ulta Pesh is stretched and sounds like a stretched Wow.

mcqs.why: Khari Zair is the standing (vertical) zair placed in zair's location, so it is written as in بِهٖ, as the book's answer explains.

mcqs.why: The book states that in place of a Khara Zabar, a small symbol of alif is placed, because its stretched sound is like the sound of alif.

lessons.title: Madd and Shadd (Tashdeed)
lessons.notes_html:
What is Madd?

Literally, the word Madd means to stretch. Madd is of two types: the long Madd and the short Madd.

  • The long Madd is stretched to the extent of 5 alif.
  • The short Madd is extended to the limit of three alif.

What is Shadd (Tashdeed)?

Shadd (Tashdeed) is a sign which looks like three teeth ( ّ ). The harf on which a Shadd is placed is called harf-e-mushaddad (Mushaddad harf), such as the Daal in مَدَّ and the Laam in حَلَّ. A Mushaddad harf is pronounced with stress; we press the sound a little while reading it.

Key Points

  • Madd means stretch; it has two types — long Madd (5 alif) and short Madd (3 alif).
  • The Shadd sign looks like three teeth ( ّ ).
  • A harf carrying a Shadd is called Mushaddad and is read with stress.

mcqs.why: The book states that the short Madd is extended to the limit of three alif, while the long Madd is stretched to 5 alif.

lessons.title: Huroof-e-Muqata'at and Pronunciation Marks (Rumooz-e-Auqaaf)
lessons.notes_html:
Huroof-e-Muqata'at

The huroof written at the start of some surahs, like المصٓ, حمٓ عسق and طسمٓ, are called Huroof-e-Muqata'at. There are 14 surahs in the Holy Quran which start with these huroof, and the prescribed way to read them is by pronouncing each of the huroof separately.

Rumooz-e-Auqaaf (Pronunciation Marks)

Rumooz-e-Auqaaf are those signs which are written in the Holy Quran and they inform the reader as to where to stop while reciting. Some of the famous signs are Waqf-e-Taam, Waqf-e-Lazim, Waqf-e-Mutlaq and Waqf-e-Jaiz.

  • The circle sign shows that the verse has finished — this is Waqf-e-Taam.
  • The sign م shows Waqf-e-Lazim — pausing here is necessary.
  • The sign لا shows La Waqfa Alaihi — not pausing here is necessary.
  • The sign ج shows Waqf-e-Jaiz — it is better to pause here, and not pausing here is also permissible.

Al-Sajda

At some places in the Holy Quran, the word 'Al-Sajda' is mentioned at the end of some verses. It means that a person needs to prostrate (perform sajda) after completing the verse.

Key Points

  • Huroof-e-Muqata'at come at the start of 14 surahs and are read letter by letter.
  • Rumooz-e-Auqaaf tell the reader where to stop during recitation.
  • 'Al-Sajda' at the end of a verse means: prostrate after completing the verse.

Learn these three surahs by heart with correct pronunciation, and recite them to your teacher.

lessons.title: Introduction to Tauheed, Risalat and Akhirat
lessons.notes_html:
The Three Basic Beliefs of Islam

There are three basic beliefs which form the foundation of Islam. It is necessary for every single person to believe in them to become a Muslim:

  • Belief in Monotheism — Aqeeda-e-Tauheed
  • Belief in Prophethood — Aqeeda-e-Risalat
  • Belief in Hereafter — Aqeeda-e-Akhirat

Tauheed (Monotheism)

Believing in heart that Allah Almighty is 'One' and stating it with the tongue is called Tauheed. Allah Almighty has no partner; He does not have any parents nor any children, and no one is like Him. All creatures are dependent upon Him for their existence.

Risalat (Prophethood)

Risalat means that Allah Almighty has selected certain people, known as Ambiya, to deliver His teaching to humankind. The Ambiya are extremely truthful; they never lie, never indulge in sin, and deliver the orders of Allah Almighty to the people. Four famous Ambiya are Hazrat Adam, Hazrat Nooh, Hazrat Ibrahim and Hazrat Moosa (peace be upon them). In the end, our beloved Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) was sent as the last Nabi.

Akhirat (Hereafter)

Akhirat is the day of judgement, on which people will be resurrected after their death and every individual will be accountable for his/her deeds. Those who did good deeds will live in the gardens of heaven, and those who committed bad deeds will be thrown in the hellfire.

Key Points

  • The three basic beliefs are Tauheed, Risalat and Akhirat.
  • Allah Almighty is One; He has no partner, no parents and no children.
  • Ambiya are the pious people sent by Allah to deliver His teachings.
  • On the day of Akhirat, everyone will be accountable for his/her deeds.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Holy Quran and Manners of Recitation
lessons.notes_html:
The Four Special Books

Allah Almighty revealed four special books upon His Rasools:

  • Toraat (Old Testament) was revealed on Hazrat Moosa (peace be upon him).
  • Zaboor (Psalms) was revealed on Hazrat Daud (peace be upon him).
  • Injeel (New Testament) was revealed on Hazrat Issa (peace be upon him).
  • The Holy Quran was revealed on our beloved Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH).

What is Tilaawat?

Tilaawat refers to reading anything which is written; however, normally this word is used for the recitation of the Holy Quran and not for other books. Ten rewards of good deeds are awarded for reciting a single letter (harf) from the Holy Quran.

Manners of Tilaawat (Recitation)

  • We need to cleanse ourselves by performing ablution (wudu) before recitation.
  • When starting Tilaawat, one should start by reciting Aaoozubillah and Bismillah completely.
  • The Holy Quran should be recited slowly, and it should be kept at a high place.
  • When hearing recitation of the Holy Quran, one should be silent and listen attentively.

Key Points

  • Toraat — Hazrat Moosa; Zaboor — Hazrat Daud; Injeel — Hazrat Issa; Quran — Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH).
  • Tilaawat normally means recitation of the Holy Quran.
  • Ten rewards are given for reciting one letter of the Holy Quran.
  • Perform wudu before recitation and begin with Aaoozubillah and Bismillah.

lessons.title: Namaz: Its Time and Manners
lessons.notes_html:
Upon Whom is Namaz Compulsory?

Namaz is compulsory for every sane Muslim who has attained puberty; all Muslim males and females should offer Namaz. On the day of judgement, the first question will be asked about the Namaz. Allah Almighty becomes happy with those who pray and angry with those who do not pray. Namaz in congregation has more thawab (reward) than praying at home.

Times of the Five Namaz

  • Fajr — from the dawn (Subh-e-Sadiq) before the sun rises.
  • Zuhr — after the sun passes its zenith until the time of 'Asr starts.
  • Asr — after the time of Zuhr ends till the sun sets.
  • Maghrib — its time starts when the sun sets.
  • Isha — when the time of Maghrib finishes, after one hour of the sun setting, Isha time starts and continues till dawn.

Manners of Namaz

For Namaz, purity is necessary of three types:

  • Purify the clothes — clothes need to be pure (clean).
  • Purify the body with Ablution (Wudu).
  • Stand on a pure (clean) place facing the Qiblah.
  • Focus humbly on Allah Almighty during Namaz; the sight should be at the place of prostration, not here and there.

Key Points

  • Namaz is compulsory for every sane Muslim who has attained puberty.
  • The first question on the day of judgement will be about Namaz.
  • Fajr is prayed at dawn, before sunrise; Maghrib starts at sunset.
  • Purity of clothes, body (wudu) and place is necessary for Namaz.

lessons.notes_html:
What is the Qiblah?

The direction which the Muslims face for offering the Namaz is known as the Qiblah. The Qiblah of Muslims is the Khana-e-Kaabah, and all Muslims face the direction of this house of Allah Almighty when they offer Namaz.

Baitullah — the House of Allah

  • Baitullah means House of Allah Almighty; it is the other name of the Khana-e-Kaabah.
  • Khana-e-Kaabah is located in Masjid-ul-Haram, which is in Makkah Mukarramah. This place is dearer to Allah Almighty than all other places.
  • Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) constructed the Khana-e-Kaabah, along with his son Hazrat Ismaeel (peace be upon him).
  • Hajar-e-Aswad is placed in the corner of the Khana-e-Kaabah.
  • The people who perform Hajj or Umrah kiss the Hajar-e-Aswad according to the Sunnah of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH).

Key Points

  • The Qiblah is the direction faced in Namaz; our Qiblah is the Khana-e-Kaabah.
  • Baitullah means the House of Allah Almighty.
  • The Kaabah is in Masjid-ul-Haram, Makkah Mukarramah.
  • Hazrat Ibrahim and Hazrat Ismaeel (peace be upon them) constructed the Khana-e-Kaabah.

lessons.title: Importance and Respect of a Masjid
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Masjid?

Masjid refers to a place of prostration. It is the place where Muslims get together to pray five times a day collectively, recite the Holy Quran and remain in the remembrance of Allah Almighty. Masajid are the houses of Allah Almighty, and the most beloved places to Allah Almighty are the Masajid; constructing Masajid yields great thawab (reward). As long as you stay in a Masjid, remain in ablution (wudu).

The First Masjid — Masjid-e-Quba

When our beloved Nabi Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) immigrated from Makkah Mukarramah to Madinah Munawwarah, he first stayed in a village near Madinah named Quba and built a Masjid there, which is famous as Masjid-e-Quba. The Nabi Karim (PBUH) himself participated in the construction of the Masajid at Quba and Madinah Munawwarah. Masjid-e-Nabawi, built after Masjid-e-Quba, is located in Madinah Munawwarah.

The Most Eminent Masajid

  • Among all the Masajid, Masjid-ul-Haraam (Kabatullah Masjid) is the most eminent.
  • After it comes Masjid-e-Nabawi.
  • After that comes Masjid Al-Aqsa, which is located in Palestine.

Key Points

  • Masjid means a place of prostration; Masajid are the houses of Allah.
  • The first Masjid, Masjid-e-Quba, was built at Quba near Madinah Munawwarah.
  • Masjid-e-Nabawi is in Madinah Munawwarah and Masjid Al-Aqsa is in Palestine.
  • Masjid-ul-Haraam is the most eminent of all Masajid.

lessons.notes_html:
Birth of the Nabi Karim (PBUH)

  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) was born in Makkah Mukarramah, a city of Arabia where the house of Allah Almighty, the Kaaba, is located. He was born in the early hours of the morning.
  • He was born in the month of Rabi-ul-Awwal.
  • He belonged to the family of Banu Hashim, which is a branch of the Quraish. The Quraish tribe was seen with a lot of respect among the Arabs.

His Blessed Family

  • Hazrat Abdullah — his respected father.
  • Hazrat Aamina — his respected mother.
  • Hazrat Abdul Muttalib — his respected grandfather.
  • Hazrat Fatima bint Asad — his respected paternal aunt.
  • Hazrat Abu Talib — his respected paternal uncle.
  • Hazrat Halima Sadia — his nursing lady.

Guardianship of Abu Talib

When the Nabi Karim (PBUH) was born, his grandfather Abdul Muttalib took him straight to the Khana-e-Kaabah and prayed for him there. After a few days, following the custom of the Arabs, he handed the child over to Hazrat Halima (may Allah be pleased with her), who had come to Makkah Mukarramah from her village searching for children to nurse. When Abdul Muttalib was about to pass away, he gave the responsibility of his blessed grandchild to his son Abu Talib, who took care of his lovely nephew and loved him more than his sons.

Key Points

  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) was born in Makkah Mukarramah in Rabi-ul-Awwal.

lessons.title: Hilf-ul-Fudul
lessons.notes_html:
What is Hilf-ul-Fudul?

The word 'Hilf' (حلف) means agreement. 'Al-Fudul' is the plural of 'Al-Fadl'. The agreement was named Hilf-ul-Fudul because the people who helped to reach the consensus on this agreement had the word Fadl in the beginning of their names.

Why was the Agreement Made?

Incidentally, a man from the Zubaid tribe came to Makkah Mukarramah with some business goods. 'Aas bin Waail purchased some goods from him but refused to make the payment. The stranger cried: "I am a stranger, help me." Then the respectable leaders of the Quraish gathered at the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'aan, who was a pious and philanthropist person, and made this agreement. The Nabi Karim (PBUH) also participated in it.

Aim of the Agreement

  • Innocent victims would be helped against the cruel people.
  • They would not let any unjust person live in Makkah Mukarramah.

What the Nabi Karim (PBUH) Said

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) said that even if he was offered crimson camels in exchange for this agreement, he would have rejected the offer; and even today, if he is asked to participate in an agreement like Hilf-ul-Fudul, he is ready to accept it.

Key Points

  • Hilf means agreement; Al-Fudul is the plural of Al-Fadl.
  • The agreement was made at Abdullah ibn Jud'aan's house.
  • Its aim was to help innocent victims against the cruel.
  • 'Aas bin Waail had refused to pay the Zubaid trader for his goods.

Sadiq and Ameen

The Marriage

lessons.notes_html:
The Kaaba is Damaged

Once it rained a lot and the Khana-e-Kaabah was filled with rain water, which damaged its structure. So the Quraish decided to construct (rebuild) the Khana-e-Kaabah.

The Fight Between the Tribes

The tribes fought on fixing the Hajar-e-Aswad back in the wall. The leader of each tribe wanted the honour of fixing Hajar-e-Aswad for himself, so there was a fight amongst the tribes.

The Wise Decision

To end the conflict, it was decided that whoever came into the Khana-e-Kaabah first, he would decide how to end this conflict. With the grace of Allah Almighty, it was the Nabi Karim (PBUH) who entered the Kaaba first. When the people saw him, they exclaimed: "The Ameen (trustworthy) is here, and we will be happy with his decision."

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) decided to place the Hajar-e-Aswad on a blanket, which would be lifted by the leaders of all the tribes. All the leaders happily accepted his suggestion, and with his vision and strategy the conflict ended.

Key Points

  • Heavy rain damaged the Khana-e-Kaabah, so the Quraish rebuilt it.
  • The tribes fought over the honour of fixing Hajar-e-Aswad in the wall.
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) entered first and was chosen to decide.
  • He placed the stone on a blanket lifted by all the tribal leaders, ending the conflict.

lessons.title: Isolation in the Cave of Hira
lessons.notes_html:
Mount Noor and the Cave of Hira

  • Mount Noor (Jabl-e-Noor) is located on the eastern side of Makkah Mukarramah, at a distance of 4 km from Masjid-ul-Haraam.
  • The Cave of Hira is located on the top of Mount Noor, at a height of 632 meters.

Why did he go to the Cave?

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) went to the Cave of Hira to stay away from other people and remain in isolation. Over there, he would remain busy with the remembrance of Allah Almighty and with pondering upon the greatness of Allah and the condition of his people, safe from the evils of the society. Before the bestowment of Nabi-hood, he was inclined towards remaining in isolation.

The First Revelation

  • The angel who brought revelation was Hazrat Jibrael (peace be upon him); through him the message of Allah reached the Nabi Karim (PBUH).
  • The first revelation was revealed upon the Nabi Karim (PBUH) in the Cave of Hira, and this revelation was the initial part of the Holy Quran.
  • When Nabi-hood was bestowed upon him, his age was 40 years.
  • He was made a Nabi after the arrival of the revelation; then he taught the people about Tauheed (Monotheism).

Key Points

  • The Cave of Hira is on top of Mount Noor, 4 km from Masjid-ul-Haraam.

  • Hazrat Jibrael (peace be upon him) brought the first revelation there.

lessons.title: Truthfulness, Trustworthiness and Best Practices of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH)
lessons.notes_html:
Al-Sadiq — the Truthful

The people of Makkah Mukarramah entitled the Nabi Karim (PBUH) as 'Al-Sadiq' (the Truthful), because he always spoke the truth and never lied in his life. When he climbed upon Mount Safa and invited the people towards Tauheed, they replied: "You have never told a lie." Even Abu Jahl said: "I do not call you a liar."

Lying — a Sign of a Hypocrite

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) said that there are three signs of a hypocrite, and one of them is that he always lies when he speaks. So telling lies is a sign of a hypocrite, and we should always speak the truth.

Trustworthiness — Returning the Trusts

When the polytheists of Makkah Mukarramah besieged the house of the Nabi Karim (PBUH), he nominated Hazrat Ali Al-Murtaza (may Allah be pleased with him) to return the trusts of the people; he gave those trusts to Hazrat Ali and told him to hand them over to their owners in the morning.

Husn-e-Muaamalaat — the Best Practices

Conducting transactions and all other matters in the best way, and doing well for others, is called Husn-e-Muaamalaat (the Best Practices). In matters like sale and purchase and financial dealings, the character of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) was pure and exalted. This practice of his is a great example of his Husn-e-Muaamalaat.

Key Points

  • Al-Sadiq means the Truthful; the people of Makkah gave him this title.
  • Lying when speaking is one of the three signs of a hypocrite.
  • He returned the people's trusts through Hazrat Ali (may Allah be pleased with him).
  • Dealing with others in the best way is called Husn-e-Muaamalaat.

lessons.title: Tolerance, Patience and Social Excellence of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH)
lessons.notes_html:
Rawadari (Tolerance)

'Rawadari' (Tolerance) means that if a person has some difference of opinion on a certain matter or belief, then he/she respects the belief or opinion of the other person. That person should not be forced to leave his/her belief or opinion and accept your belief or opinion. In religion there is no compulsion.

An example: the Nabi Karim (PBUH) hosted a delegation of Christians in the Masjid-e-Nabawi and allowed them to pray as per their religion.

Sabr wa Tahammul (Patience)

'Sabr wa Tahammul' (Patience) means that if you are hurt by anyone in any way, you bear the pain and do not take revenge even if you have the power to do it; and you never complain about it, not even a little. Allah Almighty is with the patient people (Surah Al-Baqarah: 153).

Husn-e-Ma'asharat (Social Excellence)

Hazrat Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates that he served the Nabi Karim (PBUH) for ten years. During this time he made some mistakes which caused some big as well as small losses to the Nabi Karim (PBUH), yet the Nabi Karim (PBUH) never became angry with him. In another example of Husn-e-Ma'asharat, the Nabi Karim (PBUH) said about a villager: you people should side with him, as he has the right to speak.

Key Points

  • Rawadari (Tolerance) means respecting the belief or opinion of others.
  • The Christian delegation was hosted in Masjid-e-Nabawi and allowed to pray.
  • Patience means bearing pain without revenge and without complaint.
  • Hazrat Anas served the Nabi Karim (PBUH) for ten years and he never became angry with him.

lessons.notes_html:
Siblings Have Rights Upon One Another

In our family, after our parents, the relation that comes is of brothers and sisters. Brothers and sisters have mutual rights upon each other, which should be fulfilled. Keeping good relations with brothers and sisters makes us prosperous in the world and in the hereafter, and keeps us safe from many problems.

Duty of the Youngers towards the Elders

  • The youngers should respect their elders.
  • They should obey their elders.
  • They should respect the elders like their parents, sit with them respectfully, and behave well with them.

Duty of the Elders towards the Youngers

  • The elders should show compassion and love for the youngers like a father.
  • They should take care of their needs, education and upbringing.

Hadith

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) said: "He is not one of us who does not have mercy on young children and does not respect the elders."

Key Points

Who are our Relatives?

Our relatives include our paternal uncles and aunts and our maternal uncles and aunts, along with their children — our nieces, nephews and cousins. Our relatives do not include only the paternal uncle and aunt; the maternal side is also included.

How to Treat Relatives

  • If a relative has a valid need, we should try our best to fulfil it.
  • If you want to spend in the way of Allah Almighty, first spend on your relatives, because they have the most right.

Hadith

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) said: "The paternal uncle and father are two branches of the same tree." So the paternal uncle is like the father, and his rights are similar to the rights of the father.

Key Points

  • Relatives include paternal and maternal uncles and aunts, nieces, nephews and cousins.
  • We should fulfil the valid needs of our relatives.
  • Spending in the way of Allah should begin with our relatives.
  • The paternal uncle is like the father; his rights are like the father's rights.

Our companions, who stay together with us for a while, have rights similar to neighbors, for example the students studying in a class together, or the people of the same profession who stay together for some time.

Three Types of Neighbors in the Holy Quran

  • Neighbors who are relatives.
  • Neighbors who are not relatives.
  • People who stay together for a while (companions).

Teachings of the Nabi Karim (PBUH)

  • A woman who used to fast the whole day and pray the whole night but misbehaved with her neighbor — the Nabi Karim (PBUH) said she will go to hell.
  • "He has no right to be called a believer who fills his belly while his neighbor remains hungry."
  • About the broth (gravy), the Nabi Karim (PBUH) said: put plenty of water in it, so that the neighbor may also be given from it.
  • Fighting and quarrels between neighbors make life miserable.

Key Points

  • Companions have rights similar to neighbors.
  • The Quran mentions three types of neighbors.
  • Misbehaving with a neighbor destroys the reward of worship.
  • A believer does not eat his fill while his neighbor stays hungry.

lessons.title: Avoid Lying
lessons.notes_html:
Truth is the Best Habit

The antonym of lie is truth. Speaking the truth is the best habit, and it has been the primary quality of every Nabi (peace be upon them). A person should always speak the truth, because speaking the truth leads towards a path of goodness. Allah Almighty says: "The curse of Allah be on the liars."

Harms of Lying

  • People stop trusting a person who tells lies.
  • The liar's status is lowered among the people; he loses his honour.
  • A student who lies loses his honour among his class fellows, and the affection and respect of his teachers is taken away.
  • A liar is a sinner in front of Allah Almighty.

Remember

  • Lying is a sign of the hypocrites.
  • A believer has no relation with lying.
  • Islam has included lying among the worst bad habits.

  • The antonym of lie is truth; truthfulness is the best habit.
  • Truthfulness was the primary quality of every Nabi.
  • People stop trusting a liar and his status is lowered.
  • Lying is a sign of the hypocrites; a believer never lies.

lessons.notes_html:
What is Theft?

Theft means to take or use a protected item without the permission of its owner. Theft is considered a very bad deed in every society and every religion. Islam has fixed a severe punishment for the person who steals.

Hadith

The Nabi Karim (PBUH) said: "When a thief steals, his faith leaves him at that time."

More Teachings

  • Entering a person's home without his permission is extremely bad.
  • Many other bad things are hidden in theft.
  • When we save ourselves from theft and instruct others to stay away from it, our society becomes a place of peace.

lessons.title: Refraining from Backbiting and Accusation
lessons.notes_html:
Gheebat (Backbiting)

Gheebat (backbiting) means to state the bad things or habits of a person in his absence. Backbiting is not done by the tongue only; it also includes revealing someone's faults, pointing with the eyes, and gestures with the hand.

Buhtan (Accusation)

Buhtan (accusation) means to accuse a person of things which he has not committed. Buhtan is worse and more dangerous than Gheebat.

Harms of Both

  • Both Gheebat and Buhtan hurt the feelings of a person and invoke the anger of Allah Almighty.
  • The Holy Quran gives the example: backbiting is like eating the flesh of his dead brother (Surah Al-Hujuraat: 12).
  • Hurting someone's feelings and insulting someone is an unforgivable sin unless the victim forgives.

Key Points

  • Gheebat is stating a person's faults in his absence.
  • Buhtan is accusing a person of what he did not do.
  • Buhtan is worse and more dangerous than Gheebat.
  • Backbiting is like eating the flesh of one's dead brother.

lessons.title: Manners of Conversation
lessons.notes_html:
The Command of the Holy Quran

Allah Almighty says in the Holy Quran (Surah Al-Baqarah: 83):

وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا

"And talk to the people in the best manner" — meaning we should talk to people softly and with love.

How the Nabi Karim (PBUH) Spoke

  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) used to speak slowly, in a very soft voice.
  • His words could be counted; his talk was clear and easily understood by everyone.
  • When needed, he would repeat a thing three times.

Manners we should Follow

  • Speak softly and with love; soft and loving speech cajoles others to be nice and soft.
  • With the elders, speak with respect.
  • When someone is talking, listen with complete focus and attention.
  • There should be no harshness in conversation; talk according to need only and avoid futile and uncivilized talks.

Key Points

  • The Quran commands: talk to the people in the best manner.
  • The Nabi Karim (PBUH) spoke slowly and softly; his words could be counted.
  • Listen with complete focus when someone talks.
  • Avoid harshness and useless talk; speak only according to need.

lessons.title: Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him)
lessons.notes_html:
His Father Aazar

The name of the father of Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was Aazar. Aazar was a polytheist; he used to make statues and was the chief priest of the temple. The people used to worship the statues.

Hazrat Ibrahim's Thinking

Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used to think that the statue which Aazar has made by his own hands, how can it become a god? The statues have no authority or power at all. He tried to make the people understand about the Oneness of Allah Almighty.

Breaking the Statues

Once, when everyone had gone to the festival, Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) entered the temple, where there was one big statue and many small statues. He broke the small statues to pieces with an axe and hanged the axe on the hand of the big statue. When the people came back and saw this, they were ashamed of themselves, but they remained steadfast on polytheism.

Key Points

  • Aazar, the father of Hazrat Ibrahim, made statues and was chief priest of the temple.
  • Hazrat Ibrahim knew that a statue made by hands cannot be a god.
  • He broke the small statues and hanged the axe on the big statue's hand.
  • He called the people towards the Oneness of Allah Almighty.

lessons.title: Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him)
lessons.notes_html:
His Name and Family

  • His name was Abdullah, and his father's name was Usman, who was famous by his kunniyat Abu Qahafa.
  • He was a businessman who dealt in garments (clothes).
  • His daughter Hazrat Aisha Siddiqa (may Allah be pleased with her) became the wife of the Nabi Karim (PBUH).

The Title 'Siddiq'

When the Nabi Karim (PBUH) invited him towards Islam, he accepted Islam immediately. He got the title of 'Siddiq' because he believed and confirmed the incident of Mairaj (the ascension of the Nabi Karim (PBUH)). 'Siddiq' means the one who always confirms (the truth).

Companion of the Prophet (PBUH)

  • He was the closest companion of the Nabi Karim (PBUH) and remained with him most of the time.
  • He accompanied the Nabi Karim (PBUH) on the journey of Hijrat towards Madinah Munawwarah; on the way they stayed in the Cave of Thawr for three days and three nights.
  • During the last illness of the Nabi Karim (PBUH), he was ordered to lead the Namaz in his place.

The First Caliph

After the demise of the Nabi Karim (PBUH), the Companions chose Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) as the Caliph (Khalifa) and ruler. He passed away at the age of 63 years.

Key Points

  • His name was Abdullah; his father Usman was known as Abu Qahafa.
  • He accepted Islam immediately when invited.
  • He got the title Siddiq for confirming the incident of Mairaj.
  • He stayed with the Prophet (PBUH) in the Cave of Thawr for three days and three nights.
  • After the Prophet's demise, he became the first Caliph.
